note: Proportions per pound of flour, which is how a bench thinks. The raised dough is the Wikibooks recipe's own ratios, converted to the pound and kept under CC BY-SA. The others say plainly that the proportions are this project's, because no free-to-use version was found.
house_note: A pound of flour is about a dozen donuts, cut at three and a half inches. That conversion is this project's rule of thumb, not a measurement — a shop cuts thinner or thicker and gets a different count.

meats.note: two dozen, and a long morning

levels.name: Cake batter
levels.says: Lifted by baking powder, mixed soft, dropped straight into the fat. About 90 seconds, turning once.

anchor.note: This project's own proportions. No free-to-use cake-donut recipe was found to build on. What is cited is what a cake donut IS: cake flour at 7 to 8 percent protein, chemical leavening, extra shortening in the batter, fried 190–198 °C.

when: Beat the sugar, egg and melted shortening, then the buttermilk.
Fold in the flour, baking powder, salt and nutmeg. Stop when it comes together.
Chill the batter at least an hour. Warm batter will not hold a ring.
Drop rings into 190–198 °C fat. Turn once when the underside sets.
About 90 seconds in all. Sugar them warm, not hot.

levels.name: Raised dough
levels.says: Yeast, two rises, about 150 seconds in the fat at 182–190 °C. The dough that sets the shop's clock.

anchor.title: Cookbook:Doughnuts (Yeasted)
anchor.note: The recipe's own quantities — 5 cups flour, 1½ cups milk, ½ cup sugar, ⅓ cup shortening, 2 eggs, 2 envelopes of yeast — converted to the pound of flour. The recipe itself notes that two envelopes is a lot of yeast and will taste of it.

when: Scald the milk to 180 °F, then cool it below 105 °F.
Sprinkle the yeast over the warm water and leave it five minutes.
Mix the yeast, milk, sugar, salt, eggs, shortening and a third of the flour. Beat in the rest until the dough leaves the bowl. Knead five minutes.
Rise in a greased covered bowl until doubled — a dent should stay when you press it.
Roll to half an inch, cut with a floured cutter, and let the cut rings rise again until doubled.
Fry at 182–190 °C, about 150 seconds, turning once. Glaze within a minute of the fat.

levels.name: Potato dough
levels.says: Riced potato in a raised dough: softer crumb, keeps longer. Spudnuts and fasnachts.

anchor.note: This project's own proportions, built off the raised dough above. What is cited is the practice — Pennsylvania Dutch fasnachts are often potato donuts, and the Spudnut franchise was built on a dry potato mix.

when: Boil, rice and cool the potato. Lumps become holes.
Build the dough as for raised, with the potato going in at the milk stage.
Expect a slacker dough. Flour the bench, not the dough.
Cut square or diamond with a slit if you are making fasnachts; rings otherwise.
Fry as for raised. It browns a shade faster.

levels.name: Choux paste
levels.says: No yeast, no powder. Steam lifts it and it fries hollow — the French cruller.

anchor.note: This project's own proportions. What is cited is what a French cruller IS: choux pastry — flour cooked into butter and water, then beaten with eggs — extruded in a ring and fried.

when: Boil the water and butter. Beat in all the flour at once and cook it until it pulls from the pan.
Cool it a few minutes, then beat the eggs in one at a time until it ribbons.
Pipe rings onto squares of paper through a star tip.
Slide them in paper and all; the paper lifts off once they set.
Fry until deep gold. Underdone choux collapses. Glaze thin.
